title: The effective and responsible arial application of agrochemical products

lessons.title: When and why to apply agrochemicals from the air
lessons.html:
Aerial application in South African agriculture

Aerial application by fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters and, increasingly, drones (remotely piloted aircraft) is used where ground rigs are too slow or cannot enter: large maize, soybean and wheat fields, sugarcane, forestry plantations, wet lands after rain, and tall crops late in the season. It is fast and does not compact soil or damage crops with wheel tracks, but drift risk is higher and mistakes affect large areas quickly.

Legal framework

  • Agricultural remedies must be registered under the Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act 36 of 1947, and used only as the label directs. The label must specifically allow aerial application for the product to be applied from the air.
  • Aircraft, pilots and drone operators must be licensed by the South African Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) for the operation concerned.
  • Pest control operators who apply remedies for reward must be registered as required under Act 36 of 1947.
  • Worker safety falls under the OHS Act 85 of 1993 and its regulations on hazardous chemical agents.

Deciding whether aerial application is right

Ask: is the pest at an economic threshold? Is the product registered for aerial use on this crop? Can drift be controlled given sensitive areas nearby (homes, schools, rivers, organic farms, beehives, vineyards near cotton or maize treated with hormone herbicides)? Is a ground or drone application a safer alternative? Integrated pest management should be considered first, with chemicals as one tool among others.

The farm manager, the aerial operator and the agronomist share responsibility. A written job order specifying field, crop, product, rate, water volume, timing and buffer zones prevents misunderstandings.

lessons.title: Planning the application and controlling drift
lessons.html:
Accuracy and drift control

Pre-application planning

  1. Map the field with GPS boundaries and mark sensitive areas, power lines, trees and obstacles.
  2. Confirm product, rate per hectare, total volume and any adjuvant, all as per the label.
  3. Agree buffer zones from water bodies, houses and sensitive crops. Respect any buffers stated on the label.
  4. Notify neighbours and beekeepers ahead of time.
  5. Arrange a safe loading site away from water, with spill kits and PPE.
  6. Plan flight lines, usually across the wind.

Weather conditions

Drift is mainly controlled by droplet size and weather.

  • Wind: do not spray in strong wind, or in completely still air. Follow the label and operator's standards.
  • Temperature inversions: on calm, clear early mornings and evenings, cool air near the ground traps fine droplets that can drift long distances. Avoid spraying under inversion conditions.
  • High temperature and low humidity cause evaporation and smaller droplets that drift further.

Record wind speed and direction, temperature and humidity at the start and during the application.

Droplet size and equipment

Coarser droplets drift less but may give less coverage; nozzles, pressure and aircraft speed are selected to give the droplet spectrum the label and target require. Calibrate the system so that the actual rate matches the planned rate. Flag or GPS guidance ensures correct swath overlap without gaps or double dosing.

Drones

Drones fly lower and treat smaller areas, which can reduce drift, but they still need registration of the operation, a licensed pilot, label approval and the same weather discipline.

lessons.title: Safety, records and evaluating results
lessons.html:
Protecting people and the environment

Ground crew and workers

  • Loaders wear the PPE on the label: chemical-resistant gloves, coveralls, boots, face shield or goggles and respirator where required.
  • Use closed transfer systems where possible to reduce exposure.
  • Never use flaggers standing in the spray path without proper protection; GPS guidance is preferred.
  • Keep workers out of treated fields until the re-entry period on the label has passed.
  • Have clean water, soap and an eyewash available; know the poison information numbers and nearest clinic. If someone is exposed, remove contaminated clothing, wash the skin with lots of water and take the label to the doctor.

Spills and disposal

Contain spills with absorbent material, keep them out of drains and water, and dispose of contaminated material and empty containers through approved channels. Triple-rinse containers into the spray tank and puncture them so they cannot be reused for water or food.

Records

Keep a full application record: date and time, field, crop and growth stage, target pest, product and registration number, rate and volume, weather readings, operator and aircraft, and pre-harvest interval. Records support residue compliance for markets and are your evidence if drift damage is claimed.

Evaluating effectiveness

Scout the field after the planned interval to check pest control and crop safety. Compare treated and untreated strips where possible. Poor results may come from wrong timing, resistance, poor coverage or rain washing off the product. Rotate modes of action to delay resistance.

Handling complaints

Investigate any drift complaint promptly, check records and wind data and, where needed, take samples. Good neighbour relations are part of responsible application.

Key points

  • Apply from the air only products whose label allows aerial use.
  • Use licensed aircraft and operators and registered pest control operators.
  • Avoid wind extremes and temperature inversions; use buffer zones.
  • Protect ground crew with label PPE and observe re-entry periods.
  • Keep full records and evaluate results.
